passages.text: What Do My Kidneys Do? Your kidneys are basically your body’s filtration system. Every minute, approximately half a cup of blood flows through them. As the blood flows through, waste products are removed, as is excess water; the levels of minerals and salt are also adjusted if need be. Although around 150 quarts of blood are filtered by your kidneys every day as it continually cycles through your body, only about 1-2 quarts of urine are produced from the waste products and excess water. The urine then flows to the bladder through a tube called the ureter. How Do My Kidneys Work? Inside each kidney, there are about a million tiny filtration units called nephrons. The nephrons are made up of a filter called a glomerulus and a tube called a tubule. Blood flows through the glomerulus, where waste and excess water or minerals are filtered out. The tubule then sends the filtered substances to collect in the kidneys before flowing through the ureter to the bladder, while the newly-filtered blood is returned to the rest of the body. Each of your kidneys is made up of about a million filtering units called nephrons. Each nephron includes a filter, called the glomerulus, and a tubule. The nephrons work through a two-step process: the glomerulus filters your blood, and the tubule returns needed substances to your blood and removes wastes. The glomerulus filters your blood As blood flows into each nephron, it enters a cluster of tiny blood vessels—the glomerulus. The thin walls of the glomerulus allow smaller molecules, wastes, and fluid—mostly water—to pass into the tubule. Larger molecules, such as proteins and blood cells, stay in the blood vessel. The tubule returns needed substances to your blood and removes wastes A blood vessel runs alongside the tubule. As the filtered fluid moves along the tubule, the blood vessel reabsorbs almost all of the water, along with minerals and nutrients your body needs.

They are located just below the rib cage, one on each side of your spine. Healthy kidneys filter about a half cup of blood every minute, removing wastes and extra water to make urine. The urine flows from the kidneys to the bladder through two thin tubes of muscle called ureters, one on each side of your bladder. Your bladder stores urine. Your kidneys, ureters, and bladder are part of your urinary tract. Why are the kidneys important? Your kidneys remove wastes and extra fluid from your body. Your kidneys also remove acid that is produced by the cells of your body and maintain a healthy balance of water, salts, and minerals—such as sodium, calcium, phosphorus, and potassium—in your blood. Without this balance, nerves, muscles, and other tissues in your body may not work normally. Each kidney is about the size of a fist and is responsible for filtering blood, regulating various hormones, and maintaining a proper balance of electrolytes and fluids in the body. Their intricate structure allows them to perform numerous functions that are essential for sustaining life. Firstly, kidneys filter out waste products, toxins, and excess substances from the bloodstream, transforming them into urine for elimination. This process ensures that harmful levels of chemicals do not accumulate in the body, thus supporting systemic health. Moreover, kidneys regulate hormones such as erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production, and renin, which plays a key role in blood pressure regulation. Additionally, kidneys help maintain electrolyte balance by adjusting the levels of sodium, potassium, and calcium, thereby ensuring that bodily functions proceed smoothly. Anatomy of the Kidneys The kidneys, two bean-shaped organs located in the lower back, play a crucial role in maintaining bodily balance by filtering blood and excreting waste. Each kidney consists of three main regions: the cortex, medulla, and renal pelvis. The outer layer, the cortex, contains numerous nephrons—the kidneys’ functional units. These nephrons are tasked with filtering blood, reabsorbing essential substances, and excreting the resulting waste as urine. Beneath the cortex lies the medulla, which contains renal pyramids; these cone-shaped structures contain the nephron’s loops and collecting ducts. The medulla’s pyramids funnel the filtered urine into the renal pelvis, a funnel-shaped structure that acts as a conduit to transport urine to the ureters and eventually out of the body. Nephrons are vital for kidney functionality; each kidney holds about a million nephrons. They consist of a glomerulus, a tiny blood vessel network where filtration occurs, and a tubule where reabsorption and secretion happen. Kidneys and Hormone Regulation The kidneys play a significant role beyond filtration; they are essential in the production and regulation of various hormones. Three key hormones produced by the kidneys are renin, erythropoietin, and calcitriol, each playing crucial roles in maintaining bodily functions. Renin is an enzyme that helps regulate blood pressure. When blood pressure drops, the kidneys release renin, which activates a chain of reactions that ultimately leads to the production of angiotensin II, a substance that constricts blood vessels and raises blood pressure. Sodium and Potassium Regulation Sodium is vital for maintaining blood pressure and fluid balance, while potassium is essential for nerve and muscle function. The kidneys can reabsorb or excrete these ions based on the body’s needs. For instance, when sodium levels are low, the kidneys reabsorb more sodium back into the bloodstream. Conversely, high potassium levels trigger the kidneys to excrete excess potassium, ensuring homeostasis. Acid-Base Balance The kidneys also maintain acid-base balance, crucial for metabolic processes. They help regulate blood pH by excreting hydrogen ions (H+) and reabsorbing bicarbonate. If the blood becomes too acidic, the kidneys increase bicarbonate reabsorption, counteracting acidity. Conversely, they may excrete more bicarbonate if the blood is too alkaline, stabilizing pH levels. Hormonal Regulation Hormonal signals are critical in regulating fluid balance. The first is a blood test called estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and the second is a urine test known as the urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR). Both tests are needed to have a clear picture of your kidney health. - Albumin to creatinine ratio (ACR) measures the albumin (a kind of protein) in your pee. Having too much albumin may mean your kidney’s filtering units have been damaged by disease. One positive result could be due to fever or heavy exercise, so your doctor will want to confirm your test over 3 months. - Estimated glomerular rate (eGFR) is a blood test measuring creatinine (a waste product from the digestion of dietary protein and the normal breakdown of muscle tissue) from which kidney function levels can be estimated. Aside from having kidney disease, creatinine levels can be affected by other factors, including diet, muscle (weight of your muscles), pregnancy, malnutrition, chronic illnesses, and more. Final Words The kidneys are remarkable organs that perform critical functions in our bodies, including filtering blood, regulating hormones, and maintaining balance. They filter approximately 50 gallons of blood daily, removing waste and excess substances to produce urine. This process helps maintain electrolyte balance and homeostasis, ensuring that essential minerals like sodium and potassium stay within healthy limits. Beyond filtering, kidneys play a pivotal role in hormone regulation; they produce erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production and renin to manage blood pressure. Maintaining kidney health is vital, as compromised function can lead to serious health issues like kidney disease or hypertension. Individuals should monitor their hydration, dietary intake, and blood pressure levels to support kidney performance. Regular medical check-ups that include kidney function tests can help catch potential problems early. As science evolves, new therapies and research continue to advance understanding in urology. Staying informed about kidney health and proactive in lifestyle choices is essential.
